why_how.text: SIPDE gives you a repeatable way to find hazards early and plan your response before trouble arrives.
You cannot count on others to see you, so the strategy depends on your own eyes.

scenario.text: Kim drives past a school and sees children near the curb and a car waiting to pull out.

reasoning.text: Children can make short, fast moves, and the waiting car may move into her path, so both are hazards to identify and predict.

narration.text: SIPDE is a five-step driving strategy: Scan, Identify, Predict, Decide and Execute. Each step builds on the last. You search the scene, pick out the hazards, think about what they may do, plan what you will do, and then act. This unit walks through each step in order, then closes with the idea that sits under all of them: the only eyes you can truly rely on are your own. Using the steps on every drive helps you spot trouble early and leaves you time to respond calmly instead of reacting at the last second. To restate the key point: SIPDE is a five-step driving strategy: Scan, Identify, Predict, Decide and Execute.

In the Scan step you search ahead, to the sides and behind for hazards before they arise, and you look for escape routes near intersections, shopping areas, schools and commercial zones. While scanning, look for oncoming traffic that may turn in front of you, traffic from the left and right including bicycles and pedestrians, traffic coming up behind you, and hazardous road conditions. Scanning is wide and constant. It is not a quick glance ahead, but a steady search of the whole scene around your vehicle, with an eye on where you could go if you had to move.

In the Identify step you locate the hazards you found while scanning. They include moving vehicles and pedestrians, children and animals that can make short, fast moves, and fixed objects such as potholes, guard rails and trees that also affect your driving plan. Scanning searches the whole scene, while identifying pins down which things in it are hazards. A ball rolling into the street, a child on a bike near the curb, or a pothole ahead in your lane are all examples of hazards to identify so you can plan around them. Put simply: In the Identify step you locate hazards: moving vehicles and pedestrians, children and animals that can make short, fast moves, and fixed objects such as potholes, guard rails and trees that shape your driving plan.

In the Predict step you weigh the speed, distance and direction of each hazard, and cars moving into your path matter more than ones moving away or standing still. In the Decide step you work out in advance what you would do if the situation changed quickly, and you keep making such decisions as traffic changes. Predicting is about the hazard, while deciding is about you. First you judge what the hazard is likely to do, then you choose your own response ahead of time, so you are ready if the hazard moves. Remember this rule: In the Decide step you work out in advance what you would do if the situation changed quickly, and you keep making such decisions as traffic changes.

In the Execute step you carry out your decision. You signal your presence with your lights, horn or both, and you adjust your speed, position or direction. Executing is where the earlier steps pay off. Because you scanned, identified, predicted and decided in advance, you can act smoothly instead of braking hard or swerving at the last moment. A light tap of the horn, an easing of speed, or a small move within your lane are typical ways of carrying out your plan once you have it ready. Once more: In the Decide step you work out in advance what you would do if the situation changed quickly, and you keep making such decisions as traffic changes.

In the Predict step you weigh the speed, distance and direction of each hazard, and cars moving into your path matter more than ones moving away or standing still. To restate the key point: In the Predict step you weigh the speed, distance and direction of each hazard, and cars moving into your path matter more than ones moving away or standing still.

To finish, SIPDE is Scan, Identify, Predict, Decide and Execute. Scan ahead, to the sides and behind, and look for escape routes. Identify moving vehicles and people, quick movers like children and animals, and fixed objects. Predict by weighing speed, distance and direction, paying most attention to anything moving into your path. Decide in advance what you would do, and keep deciding as traffic changes. Execute by signaling your presence and adjusting speed, position or direction. Nothing guarantees others will see you, so rely on your own eyes.

why_how.text: A safe gap gives you time to see danger, react and stop.
The gap you need grows with poor conditions and longer vehicles.

narration.text: Following distance is the space that gives you time to stop. This unit explains how to count the three-second rule using a fixed point beside the road, what to do when the count shows you are too close, and when to stretch the gap to four or five seconds. It also covers how to deal with a tailgater and what adds up to your total stopping distance, from seeing the danger to reacting to it and braking. Each part shows why a bigger gap almost always makes you safer on the road. Put simply: The three-second rule assumes a standard-length vehicle in ideal conditions; in poor road conditions or in a longer vehicle, increase the count to four or five seconds.

lines.text: Count when the car ahead passes

narration.text: For the three-second rule, pick a fixed roadside point, start counting when the vehicle ahead passes it, and if you reach the point before counting three seconds you are following too closely. Good reference points for the count include a telephone pole, signpost, tree or bridge. If you are too close, slow gradually until the gap is safe. Do not brake hard to open the gap, which can surprise the driver behind you. Just ease off and count again until you reach the point after three seconds or more. Remember this rule: Good reference points for the three-second count include a telephone pole, signpost, tree or bridge, and if you are too close, slow gradually until the gap is safe.

The three-second rule assumes a standard-length vehicle in ideal conditions. In poor road conditions or in a longer vehicle, increase the count to four or five seconds. Rain, snow or ice make stopping harder, and a longer vehicle takes more room to slow down, so both call for a larger gap. The count is simply the starting point. When conditions are less than ideal, add time rather than staying at three seconds. A longer gap also gives you a better view of the road ahead and more room to react. Once more: The three-second rule assumes a standard-length vehicle in ideal conditions; in poor road conditions or in a longer vehicle, increase the count to four or five seconds.

Here is the trap. When someone tailgates you, it is tempting to speed up or to brake hard to make them back off. Instead, ease off your speed a little and let that driver go around. Speeding up only moves you closer to the vehicle in front of you, and braking suddenly can cause a crash from behind. By slowing a little, you give the tailgater a chance to pass and you open more room ahead, which gives you more time to stop if the traffic in front of you slows down. To restate the key point: When someone tailgates you, ease off your speed a little and let that driver go around.

Stopping distance is more than braking. It grows with the time it takes you to see and recognize the danger, before the reaction time to the brake even begins. Then there is a short delay between noticing danger and putting on the brakes. Stopping distance also depends on weather, tire tread and brake condition. Wet or icy roads, worn tires and weak brakes all add distance. That is why a safe following gap matters: it covers the time to see, the time to react and the distance your vehicle needs to come to a full stop. Put simply: Stopping distance also grows with the time it takes you to see and recognize the danger, before the reaction time to the brake even begins.

Here is a quick check: the car ahead passes a tree, and you reach the same tree on the count of two. What does that tell you? Recall the three-second rule. Pick a fixed roadside point, start counting when the vehicle ahead passes it, and if you reach the point before counting three seconds you are following too closely. So the answer is that you are following too closely. If you are too close, slow gradually until the gap is safe. And if the road is in poor condition, the count should be four or five seconds, not three. To restate the key point: Good reference points for the three-second count include a telephone pole, signpost, tree or bridge, and if you are too close, slow gradually until the gap is safe.

Remember this rule: When someone tailgates you, ease off your speed a little and let that driver go around.

narration.text: Even though traffic is usually lighter at night, nearly half of all fatal traffic crashes in Minnesota happen after dark. This unit explains how to prepare for a night drive, when your headlights must be on, when to switch to low beam, how far ahead you should be able to stop, and how to handle glare from other vehicles. These rules help you see the road and help other drivers see you, without blinding them with your lights. Night driving asks for more care, and these steps give you the tools to drive safely. Once more: Even though traffic is usually lighter at night, nearly half of all fatal traffic crashes in Minnesota happen after dark.

Before a night drive, study maps and directions, check that your lights work, and make sure the windshield is clean and free of defects. Knowing your route ahead of time means you spend less time reading signs in the dark. Working lights let you see and be seen. A clean windshield reduces glare from other headlights. Because nearly half of all fatal crashes in Minnesota happen after dark, a few minutes of preparation before a night trip is well worth the time and makes the drive itself much easier. To restate the key point: Even though traffic is usually lighter at night, nearly half of all fatal traffic crashes in Minnesota happen after dark.

Headlights go on at sunset and stay on until sunrise. They are also needed in rain, snow, hail, sleet or fog, or whenever you cannot clearly see five hundred feet of road ahead. So headlights are not only for full darkness. In bad weather during the day, they help you see and help others see you. If you are unsure whether you can clearly see five hundred feet ahead, turn them on. Using headlights in these conditions is required, and it is one of the simplest things you can do to stay visible. Put simply: Headlights go on at sunset and stay on until sunrise, and are also needed in rain, snow, hail, sleet or fog or whenever you cannot clearly see five hundred feet of road ahead.

Switch to low beam whenever an oncoming vehicle is within one thousand feet, and whenever you are two hundred feet or less behind another vehicle. Low beam is required at two different distances: one thousand feet for an oncoming vehicle, but only two hundred feet when you are following one. High beams can blind other drivers, whether they are coming toward you or looking in their mirrors ahead of you. Dimming at the right distance keeps everyone able to see the road clearly. Remember this rule: Low beam is required at two different distances: one thousand feet for an oncoming vehicle, but only two hundred feet when you are following one.

Here is the trap. Many drivers mix up the two low beam distances. For an oncoming vehicle, you dim when it is within one thousand feet. When you are following another vehicle, you dim once you are two hundred feet or less behind it. The oncoming distance is much longer because your high beams shine straight into the other driver's eyes. If a question asks about a car coming toward you, think one thousand feet. If it asks about a car ahead going your way, think two hundred feet. Once more: Low beam is required at two different distances: one thousand feet for an oncoming vehicle, but only two hundred feet when you are following one.

lines.text: Use the edge line in glare

narration.text: You should be able to stop within the stretch of road your headlights light up, which for most vehicles is no more than three hundred fifty feet on high beam. If you drive faster than that allows, you may not be able to stop for something you see too late. If oncoming headlights blind you, use the white edge line of the road as your guide. For glare from behind, use a day-night mirror or adjust your mirror. These habits keep you in control when lights reduce what you can see. To restate the key point: If oncoming headlights blind you, use the white edge line of the road as your guide, and for glare from behind, use a day-night mirror or adjust your mirror.

To wrap up, nearly half of fatal crashes in Minnesota happen after dark, so prepare by studying directions, checking your lights and cleaning the windshield. Headlights go on from sunset to sunrise, in rain, snow, hail, sleet or fog, and whenever you cannot see five hundred feet ahead. Dim to low beam within one thousand feet of an oncoming vehicle and within two hundred feet when following. narration.text: Freeways are multi-lane, divided highways with limited access and no stops or cross traffic, so you can travel long distances without stopping. Getting onto one safely takes planning. This unit explains the acceleration lane, how to merge, why you should not stop on the ramp, what to do at a ramp with a Yield sign and no acceleration lane, and how ramp meters work. Each step helps you match the speed of freeway traffic and fit into it smoothly, without forcing other drivers to brake or swerve around you. Remember this rule: At the end of most freeway entry ramps an acceleration lane lets you build speed to match the traffic you are joining.

lines.text: At the end of most ramps

narration.text: At the end of most freeway entry ramps, an acceleration lane lets you build speed to match the traffic you are joining. The idea is to arrive at the freeway lane moving at about the same speed as the vehicles already on it. Entering too slowly forces other drivers to brake, and that can be dangerous on a road with no stops. Use the full length of the acceleration lane to reach a safe speed while you look for an opening, then move into the nearest lane when the gap is there. Once more: At the end of most freeway entry ramps an acceleration lane lets you build speed to match the traffic you are joining.

When merging onto a freeway, you must yield to vehicles already on it, signal, and move into a safe gap in the nearest lane. Do not stop on an entry ramp or in the acceleration lane unless it is absolutely necessary. Stopping makes merging harder, because you then have to enter from a standstill into fast traffic. Keep moving, match speed, and pick your gap. The vehicles already on the freeway have the right of way, so the responsibility for finding a safe opening is yours as the merging driver. To restate the key point: Do not stop on an entry ramp or in the acceleration lane unless it is absolutely necessary.

Here is the trap. Not every ramp has an acceleration lane. Where there is no acceleration lane and the entry ramp has a Yield sign, obey it, stop if necessary, and never force your way into traffic. Drivers used to long acceleration lanes may treat every ramp the same and expect to merge at speed. At a Yield sign ramp, you may need to stop and wait for a safe gap. That is different from the usual rule of not stopping on a ramp, because here the sign tells you to yield and stop if you must. Put simply: Do not stop on an entry ramp or in the acceleration lane unless it is absolutely necessary.

Freeway ramp meters sit about halfway down the entry ramp and usually operate at peak travel hours. It is illegal to drive through their red light. Ramp meters are used in metropolitan areas to reduce jams and crashes and to ease merging, and only one car may go on each green. So if two cars are side by side at a meter, each waits for its own green. Treat the meter like any traffic signal: stop on red, go on green, and then use the rest of the ramp to build speed for merging. narration.text: Once you are on the freeway, a few rules keep you moving safely with other traffic. This unit covers matching the speed of surrounding traffic, changing lanes, when transit buses may use the shoulder, what freeway message signs tell you, and who may use high-occupancy vehicle lanes. It then explains interchanges, which link a freeway to other roads through ramps, and the diverging diamond design, including how it changes left turns and how pedestrians cross it. Knowing these rules helps you predict what others will do. Put simply: On the freeway keep close to the speed of surrounding traffic without ever exceeding the posted limit, and stay in the right-hand lane if you are slower than others.

On the freeway, keep close to the speed of surrounding traffic without ever exceeding the posted limit, and stay in the right-hand lane if you are slower than others. To change lanes to pass or to leave the freeway, signal and make sure your path is clear before moving over. Driving much slower than traffic can be as risky as speeding, because others must keep braking or passing around you. A steady speed near the flow, kept within the limit, and careful signaled lane changes make freeway driving predictable for everyone. Remember this rule: To change lanes to pass or to leave the freeway, signal and make sure your path is clear before moving over.

Transit and metro mobility buses may drive on a freeway or expressway shoulder only when main-line traffic is under thirty-five miles per hour, never more than fifteen miles per hour faster than that traffic, and never above thirty-five miles per hour. A bus using the shoulder gives way to any traffic merging, entering or exiting, and to other vehicles already on the shoulder. So in slow traffic you may see a bus moving past on the shoulder. It must yield to you if you are entering or leaving. Once more: A bus using the shoulder gives way to any traffic merging, entering or exiting, and to other vehicles already on the shoulder.

Here is a quick check: which vehicles may use a high-occupancy lane on the freeway? Recall the rule. High-occupancy vehicle lanes are only for motorcycles, buses and vehicles carrying two or more people. So the answer is motorcycles, buses and vehicles with two or more people. A driver alone in a car stays out of the HOV lane. While you are in any freeway lane, also watch the message signs: they warn of crashes, stalled vehicles and other conditions ahead, and during an AMBER Alert they may describe a vehicle so drivers who spot it can tell law enforcement.

An interchange links a freeway to a road or to another freeway through a set of ramps, so you can change roads without disrupting traffic, and the cloverleaf is one of the designs shown in the manual. In a diverging diamond interchange, the lanes cross over at each end of the bridge, so instead of turning sharply left across opposing traffic you veer left to reach the ramp. The crossover may feel strange the first time, because you briefly drive on the left side of the bridge, but the signals and markings guide you. Put simply: In a diverging diamond interchange the lanes cross over at each end of the bridge, so instead of turning sharply left across opposing traffic you veer left to reach the ramp.

Here is the trap. Drivers used to ordinary interchanges expect to turn left across oncoming traffic. In a diverging diamond, the lanes cross over at each end of the bridge, so instead of turning sharply left across opposing traffic, you veer left to reach the ramp. Diverging diamonds also give drivers a longer sight distance at turns and make wrong-way entry to ramps extremely difficult. So the left turn becomes a gentle veer, with no oncoming lane to cross, which is the main reason the design is safer. Remember this rule: Diverging diamonds give drivers a longer sight distance at turns and make wrong-way entry to ramps extremely difficult.

Diverging diamond interchanges can cut overall traffic delays by up to sixty percent, and they have fewer, more spread-out conflict points and shorter pedestrian crossings. At a diverging diamond, pedestrians cross to the middle of the bridge and walk between the traffic lanes with protective barriers on both sides. They also give drivers a longer sight distance at turns and make wrong-way entry to ramps extremely difficult. Together, these features make the interchange both faster and safer for drivers and for people on foot.

To sum up, keep close to the speed of traffic without exceeding the limit, stay right if slower, and signal and check before changing lanes. Buses may use the shoulder only in slow traffic, under strict speed limits, and they yield to merging and exiting traffic. Once more: High-occupancy vehicle lanes are only for motorcycles, buses and vehicles carrying two or more people.

narration.text: This unit covers what to do when something goes wrong on the freeway. It explains when stopping is allowed, how to signal for help, where to place flares, why you stay with your vehicle, and why backing up is illegal. It then covers how to respond to emergency vehicles and firefighting vehicles, how to leave the freeway and handle a missed exit, and what to do after a crash, including caretaker information and exchanging details with other drivers. Each rule is meant to keep you and others out of fast-moving traffic. To restate the key point: Stopping or parking on an interstate freeway is illegal except in an emergency, and running out of fuel does not count as one, so it can bring a citation.

Stopping or parking on an interstate freeway is illegal except in an emergency, and running out of fuel does not count as one, so it can bring a citation. In a freeway emergency, park on the shoulder as far from traffic as you can. Signal for help by lifting the hood and opening the trunk, or by tying a white cloth to the antenna or a door handle, and use your hazard lights. These signals tell passing drivers and officers that you need help, while keeping you clear of the traffic lanes. Put simply: Stopping or parking on an interstate freeway is illegal except in an emergency, and running out of fuel does not count as one, so it can bring a citation.

Place any flares or reflectors from one hundred to five hundred feet behind your vehicle along the right edge of the main road. They warn approaching drivers before they reach you. Stay with your vehicle if possible, because walking in the part of the highway used by traffic is illegal and extremely dangerous. Backing up or turning around on a freeway is illegal except for emergency and road repair vehicles doing their jobs. So once you stop, signal for help, set warnings behind you, and wait with your vehicle. Remember this rule: Backing up or turning around on a freeway is illegal except for emergency and road repair vehicles doing their jobs.

narration.text: When an emergency vehicle with lights and siren comes up behind you on the freeway, signal, move to the nearest side and stop without slamming the brakes or swerving, and watch for more emergency vehicles before pulling out. Stay at least five hundred feet behind any firefighting vehicle. Sudden braking or swerving can cause a crash, so move over smoothly. Other emergency vehicles often follow the first one, which is why you check before pulling back into traffic. Give them the room they need to work. Once more: Stay at least five hundred feet behind any firefighting vehicle.

For a stopped emergency vehicle with flashing lights on the shoulder, move a lane away if you safely can, and otherwise slow down. For one coming up behind you with a siren, pull to the nearest side and stop. Drivers who stop for a vehicle parked on the shoulder can block traffic, and drivers who keep going when one approaches from behind block the emergency. Ask yourself whether it is stopped or coming. To restate the key point: For a stopped emergency vehicle with flashing lights on the shoulder, move a lane away if you safely can and otherwise slow down; for one coming up behind with a siren, pull to the nearest side and stop.

After a property-damage-only crash, move to a safe place before getting out. Then exchange driver's license and insurance information with the other drivers, write down their plate numbers, and consider swapping vehicle identification numbers too. Put simply: You can add caretaker information to your DVS record so that, after a crash, officers know someone at home depends on you.

To wrap up, stop on the interstate only in an emergency, and running out of fuel is not one. Park on the shoulder, signal for help with the hood, trunk or a white cloth, use hazard lights, set flares behind you along the right edge, and stay with your vehicle. Never back up or turn around. Pull over and stop for an emergency vehicle behind you, move over or slow for one stopped on the shoulder, and stay five hundred feet behind fire vehicles. Take the next exit if you miss yours, and after a crash, follow the crash steps. Remember this rule: Stay at least five hundred feet behind any firefighting vehicle.

why_how.text: Distraction is a leading factor in Minnesota crashes because it slows your reactions.
Phone and headphone laws, and how you handle aggressive drivers, both protect your margin of safety.

scenario.text: Jo is seventeen, has a provisional license, and hears her phone ring while driving.

reasoning.text: A driver under eighteen with an instruction permit or provisional license may not use a cell phone at all, handheld or hands-free, except to call for emergency help.

result.text: Jo lets the call go and checks her phone only after she has parked.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking texting is fine while stopped at a light or in traffic.

correction.text: Texting, emailing or going online while driving is illegal in Minnesota, including while stopped in traffic.

memory_support.text: Eyes on the road, hands on the wheel, mind on the drive.

prompt.text: An adult driver is stuck in stopped traffic and wants to send a quick text. Is that allowed?

answer.text: No, texting is illegal even while stopped in traffic.

rationale.text: The texting ban covers all drivers and still applies when traffic is stopped.

narration.text: Driver distraction is a leading factor in Minnesota crashes, accounting for at least twenty-five percent of all crashes each year. This unit explains how distraction affects you, its three types and common sources, and the laws on texting, phone use by young drivers and headphones. It then covers aggressive driving: what it usually looks like, where it comes from, and how to respond when you meet an aggressive driver. Staying focused and staying calm are both ways of protecting your margin of safety on every drive. Once more: Driver distraction is a leading factor in Minnesota crashes, accounting for at least twenty-five percent of all crashes each year.

Distracted drivers miss hazards and react more slowly, which shrinks their margin of safety. The three types of distraction are visual, taking your eyes off the road; mechanical or physical, taking your hands off the wheel; and cognitive, being lost in thought. Some activities involve all three at once. Even when your eyes are on the road, a mind lost in thought can miss a hazard. Remember the three types as eyes, hands and mind, and try to keep all three on the job of driving. To restate the key point: Distracted drivers miss hazards and react more slowly, which shrinks their margin of safety.

Distractions inside the vehicle include using a phone or GPS, reaching for items, eating and drinking, adjusting the radio, talking to passengers and reading. Even looking at a crash scene or daydreaming pulls attention away from the road. Many of these seem harmless because they take only a moment, but distracted drivers miss hazards and react more slowly. Set the radio and GPS before you go, keep items within easy reach, and save snacks for a stop. The fewer things competing for your attention, the safer you are. Put simply: Distracted drivers miss hazards and react more slowly, which shrinks their margin of safety.

Texting, emailing or going online with a phone or wireless device while driving is illegal in Minnesota, including while stopped in traffic. A driver under eighteen holding an instruction permit or provisional license may not use a cell phone at all, handheld or hands-free, except to call for emergency help. Wearing headphones or earphones in both ears at once to listen to a radio or other sound device while driving is illegal. These laws target the visual, physical and mental distractions that phones and earphones create.

lines.text: Young drivers: no phone at all

narration.text: Here is the trap. There are two different phone rules. For all drivers, texting, emailing or going online while driving is illegal, even while stopped in traffic. For drivers under eighteen with an instruction permit or provisional license, the rule is stricter: no cell phone use at all, handheld or hands-free, except to call for emergency help. If a question involves a young driver with a permit or provisional license, remember that even a hands-free call is not allowed. For other drivers, the ban covers texting and going online.

Aggressive driving usually means driving faster than nearby traffic, which leads to tailgating, abrupt lane changes often without signaling, passing on the shoulder, and glaring at or threatening others. Aggressive drivers tend to have little concern for others and show anger and frustration rooted in their own mindset rather than in other drivers' actions. So when someone drives aggressively around you, it is usually not about anything you did. Knowing that makes it easier to stay calm and avoid getting drawn into a conflict.

Here is a quick check: an adult driver is stuck in stopped traffic and wants to send a quick text. Is that allowed? Recall the texting law. Texting, emailing or going online with a phone or wireless device while driving is illegal in Minnesota, including while stopped in traffic. So the answer is no. Being stopped does not change the rule, because traffic can start moving at any moment. For a driver under eighteen with a permit or provisional license, the rule is even stricter: no phone use at all except for emergency calls.

To finish, distraction accounts for at least a quarter of Minnesota crashes and makes you miss hazards and react slowly. Its three types are visual, physical and cognitive, and sources include phones, GPS, eating, the radio, passengers and daydreaming. Texting is illegal for all drivers, even when stopped. Drivers under eighteen with a permit or provisional license may not use a phone at all except for emergencies. Headphones in both ears are illegal. Faced with an aggressive driver, never challenge them: keep clear and do not meet their eyes.

why_how.text: Loads that block your view or stick out too far can hide hazards or strike others.
Trailers change how your vehicle handles and stops, so they need extra room and care.

scenario.text: Ben is hauling lumber that extends four feet past his rear bumper on an evening trip.

reasoning.text: A load extending four feet or more past the rear needs a flag at least sixteen inches square, and at night a red lantern or lamp visible from at least five hundred feet.

result.text: Ben ties a red flag to the end of the lumber and adds a red lamp before dark.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a load may stick out a little on either side of a passenger vehicle.

correction.text: On a passenger vehicle a load may not extend past the left fender line at all, and no more than six inches past the right fender line.

memory_support.text: Front short, rear flagged, left none, right a little.

prompt.text: You are packing a car and part of the load would stick out beyond the left fender. Is that allowed?

answer.text: No, nothing may extend past the left fender line.

rationale.text: The right side allows up to six inches, but the left side allows no overhang at all.

narration.text: Loads and trailers change how your vehicle looks to others and how it handles. This unit explains when a load or a crowded front seat is illegal, how far a load may extend in front, behind and to each side, and when a rear overhang needs a flag and a lamp. It then covers pulling a camper or trailer: the following distance to keep, how to balance the load, when to check the hitch and tires, and why you should drive slower. These rules keep your load secure and your vehicle under control. Remember this rule: When pulling a camper or trailer, keep at least five hundred feet of following distance from other vehicles.

lines.text: No more than three in front

narration.text: Driving with a load or with more than three people in the front seat is illegal when it blocks your view or interferes with your control of the vehicle. You need clear sight lines through your windows and mirrors, and room to steer and brake without being crowded. If a load blocks your view out the back or side, or if passengers in front get in the way of your arms, rearrange before you drive. This rule applies to cargo and to people alike, because either one can interfere with safe driving. Once more: Driving with a load or with more than three people in the front seat is illegal when it blocks your view or interferes with control.

lines.text: Rear: four feet needs a flag

narration.text: No load on a motor vehicle may extend more than three feet ahead of its front wheels or front bumper. A load extending four feet or more past the rear needs a red, yellow or orange flag at least sixteen inches square at its end, and at night a red lantern or lamp visible from at least five hundred feet. The flag and lamp warn drivers behind you that something extends beyond your vehicle. Without them, a driver could misjudge the space and strike the end of your load. To restate the key point: No load on a motor vehicle may extend more than three feet ahead of its front wheels or front bumper.

On a passenger vehicle, a load may not extend past the left fender line, or more than six inches past the right fender line. The left side sits next to oncoming traffic and passing vehicles, so nothing may stick out there at all. The right side allows only a small overhang. Load limits differ by direction: three feet ahead of the front, a flag once the overhang behind reaches four feet, none past the left fender line, and up to six inches past the right fender line. Check all four before you drive. Put simply: On a passenger vehicle a load may not extend past the left fender line, or more than six inches past the right fender line.

lines.text: Front three feet, rear needs a flag

narration.text: Here is the trap. The load limits are different in every direction, and they are easy to mix up. In front, a load may extend no more than three feet. Behind, an overhang of four feet or more needs a flag, and at night a red lamp. On a passenger vehicle, nothing may extend past the left fender line, and no more than six inches past the right. If a question asks about the left side, the answer is none. If it asks about the right side, the answer is up to six inches. Remember this rule: No load on a motor vehicle may extend more than three feet ahead of its front wheels or front bumper.

When pulling a camper or trailer, keep at least five hundred feet of following distance from other vehicles. A loaded trailer should carry ten to fifteen percent of its weight on the hitch and sit with its floor level. A trailer adds weight and length, so you need more room to stop. Proper balance helps the trailer follow your vehicle steadily instead of swaying. Too little weight on the hitch or a tipped floor can make the trailer hard to control, especially at higher speeds or in wind. Once more: When pulling a camper or trailer, keep at least five hundred feet of following distance from other vehicles.

Here is a quick check: you are packing a car and part of the load would stick out beyond the left fender. Is that allowed? Recall the side limits. On a passenger vehicle, a load may not extend past the left fender line, or more than six inches past the right fender line. So the answer is no: nothing may extend past the left fender line. Rearrange the load so it fits, or move it to the right side if it would extend no more than six inches there. Remember that the limits differ by direction, so check the front, rear and both sides.

To sum up, a load or more than three people in front is illegal when it blocks your view or control. A load may extend no more than three feet in front, needs a flag at four feet behind and a red lamp at night, may not pass the left fender line, and may extend up to six inches past the right. With a trailer, keep five hundred feet back, put some weight on the hitch with the floor level, check the hitch, tires, lights and load after the first few miles and at every stop, and drive slower than usual. To restate the key point: No load on a motor vehicle may extend more than three feet ahead of its front wheels or front bumper.
